Not only as "ambassadors."<div eID="gen34356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34357" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beseech--</hi>entreat (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.20">2Co 5:20</reference>). He is describing his ministry, not exhorting directly.<div eID="gen34357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34358" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">you also--</hi>rather, "WE ALSO (as well as God, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.20">2Co 5:20</reference>) beseech" or "entreat you": <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.14">2Co 6:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.15">15</reference>, on to <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.1">2Co 7:1</reference>, is part of this entreaty or exhortation.<div eID="gen34358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34359" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in vain--</hi>by making the grace of God a ground for continuance in sin (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.3">2Co 6:3</reference>). entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 6 2Co 6:1-18 . His Apostolic Ministry Is Approved by Faithfulness in Exhortation, in Sufferings, in Exhibition of the Fruits of the Holy ghost: His Largeness of Heart to Them Calls for Enlargement of Their Heart to Him. Exhortations to Separation from Pollution. 1. workers together-- with God ( Ac 15:4 ; 1Co 3:9 ). Not only as "ambassadors." beseech-- entreat ( 2Co 5:20 ). He is describing his ministry, not exhorting directly. you also-- rather, "WE ALSO (as well as God, 2Co 5:20 ) beseech" or "entreat you": 2Co 6:14 , 15 , on to 2Co 7:1 , is part of this entreaty or exhortation. in vain-- by making the grace of God a ground for continuance in sin ( 2Co 6:3 ). By a life of sin, showing that the word of reconciliation has been in vain, so far as you are concerned ( He 12:15 ; Jude 4). "The grace of God" here, is "the reconciliation" provided by God's love ( 2Co 5:18 , 19 ; compare Ga 2:2 ).

For--</hi>God's own promise is the ground of our exhortation.<div eID="gen34360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34361" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he saith--</hi>God the Father saith to God the Son, and so to all believers who are regarded as one with Him.<div eID="gen34361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34362" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heard thee--</hi>In the eternal purposes of my love I have hearkened to thy prayer for the salvation of thy people (compare <reference osisRef="John.17.9">Joh 17:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.15.20">15, 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.15.24">24</reference>).<div eID="gen34362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34363" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">accepted ... accepted--</hi>The Greek of the latter is more emphatic, "well-accepted." entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17268"/><div sID="gen34365" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17268"/>3. Resuming the connection with <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.1">2Co 6:1</reference>, interrupted by the parenthetical <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.2">2Co 6:2</reference>. "Giving no offense" (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.33">1Co 10:33</reference>), "approving ourselves," and all the other participles down to <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.10">2Co 6:10</reference>, are nominatives to "we also entreat you" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.1">2Co 6:1</reference>), to show the pains he took to enforce his exhortation by example, as well as precept [Alford]. "Offense" would be given, if we were without "patience" and the other qualifications which he therefore subjoins (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.14.13">Ro 14:13</reference>). <div eID="gen34365" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 3. Resuming the connection with 2Co 6:1 , interrupted by the parenthetical 2Co 6:2 . entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17269"/><div sID="gen34366" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17269"/>4. Translate, to mark the true order of the Greek words, "in everything, as God's ministers recommending ourselves," that is, that our hearers may give our message a favorable hearing, through our consistency in every respect, not that they may glorify us. Alluding to <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">2Co 3:1</reference>, he implies, We commend ourselves, not like them by word, but by deed.<div eID="gen34366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34367" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">patience--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.12">2Co 12:12</reference>). Put first. "Pure-minded" follows (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.6">2Co 6:6</reference>). Three triplets of trials exercising the "patience" (patient endurance) follow: Afflictions (or "tribulations"), necessities, distresses (or "straits"); stripes, imprisonments, tumults; labors, watchings, fastings. The first triplet expresses afflictions generally; the second, those in particular arising from the violence of men; the third, those which he brought on himself directly or indirectly. <div eID="gen34367" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17270"/><div sID="gen34368" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17270"/><hi type="bold">5. stripes--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.23">2Co 11:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.16.23">Ac 16:23</reference>).<div eID="gen34368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34369" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">imprisonments--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.23">2Co 11:23</reference>). He had been, doubtless, elsewhere imprisoned besides at Philippi when he wrote this Epistle.<div eID="gen34369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34370" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tumults--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.13.50">Ac 13:50</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.14.5">14:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.14.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.16.22">16:22</reference>; and recently <reference osisRef="Acts.19.23-Acts.19.41">Ac 19:23-41</reference>).<div eID="gen34370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34371" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">labours--</hi>in the cause of Christ (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.23">2Co 11:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.12">Ro 16:12</reference>).<div eID="gen34371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34372" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watchings--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.27">2Co 11:27</reference>). Sleepless nights.<div eID="gen34372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34373" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fastings--</hi>The context here refers to his trials, rather than devotional exercises (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.27">2Co 11:27</reference>). Thus "foodlessness" would seem to be the sense (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.11">1Co 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.12">Php 4:12</reference>). But the usual sense of the Greek is fasts, in the strict sense; and in <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.27">2Co 11:27</reference> it is spoken of independently of "hunger and thirst." (Compare <reference osisRef="Luke.2.37">Lu 2:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.10.30">Ac 10:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.14.23">14:23</reference>). However, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.32">Mt 15:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.8.3">Mr 8:3</reference>, justify the sense, more favored by the context, foodlessness, though a rare use of the word. Gaussen remarks "The apostles combine the highest offices with the humblest exterior: as everything in the Church was to be cast in the mould of death and resurrection, the cardinal principle throughout Christianity." <div eID="gen34373" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17273"/><div sID="gen34381" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17273"/>8. Translate, "Through glory and dishonor (disgrace)," namely, from those in authority, and accruing to us present. "By," or "through evil report and good report," from the multitude, and affecting us absent [Bengel]. Regarded "as deceivers" by those who, not knowing (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.9">2Co 6:9</reference>), dishonor and give us an evil report; "as true," by those who "know" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.9">2Co 6:9</reference>) us in the real "glory" of our ministry. In proportion as one has more or less of glory and good report, in that degree has he more or less of dishonor and evil report. <div eID="gen34381" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17274"/><div sID="gen34382" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17274"/><hi type="bold">9. unknown ... yet well known--</hi>"unknown" in our true character to those who "evil report" of us, "well known" to those who hold us in "good report" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.8">2Co 6:8</reference>). Conybeare explains, "Unknown by men, yet acknowledged by God" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.12">1Co 13:12</reference>). Perhaps both God and men (believers) are intended as knowing him (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.11">2Co 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.6">11:6</reference>).<div eID="gen34382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34383" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dying ... live--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.9">2Co 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.10">4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.23">11:23</reference>). Compare Gaussen's remark, see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.5">2Co 6:5</reference>. "Behold" calls attention to the fact as something beyond all expectation.<div eID="gen34383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34384" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chastened ... not killed--</hi>realizing <reference osisRef="Ps.118.18">Psa 118:18</reference>. <div eID="gen34384" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 9. unknown ... yet well known-- "unknown" in our true character to those who "evil report" of us, "well known" to those who hold us in "good report" ( 2Co 6:8 ). Conybeare explains, "Unknown by men, yet acknowledged by God" ( 1Co 13:12 ). Perhaps both God and men (believers) are intended as knowing him ( 2Co 5:11 ; 11:6 ). dying ... live-- ( 2Co 1:9 ; 4:10 , 11 ; 11:23 ). Compare Gaussen's remark, see on 2Co 6:5 . "Behold" calls attention to the fact as something beyond all expectation. chastened ... not killed-- realizing Psa 118:18 .

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17276"/><div sID="gen34389" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17276"/><hi type="bold">11. mouth ... open unto you--</hi>I use no concealment, such as some at Corinth have insinuated (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2Co 4:2</reference>). I use all freedom and openness of speech to you as to beloved friends. Hence he introduces here, "O Corinthians" (compare <reference osisRef="Phil.4.15">Php 4:15</reference>). The enlargement of his heart towards them (<reference osisRef="2Cor.7.3">2Co 7:3</reference>) produced his openness of mouth, that is, his unreserved expression of his inmost feelings. As an unloving man is narrow in heart, so the apostle's heart is enlarged by love, so as to take in his converts at Corinth, not only with their graces, but with their many shortcomings (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.29">1Ki 4:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.32">Psa 119:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.5">Is 60:5</reference>). <div eID="gen34389" type="x-p"/>

Too close intercourse with unbelievers in other relations also is included ( 2Co 6:16 ; 1Co 8:10 ; 10:14 ). fellowship-- literally, "share," or "participation." righteousness-- the state of the believer, justified by faith. unrighteousness-- rather, as always translated elsewhere, "iniquity"; the state of the unbeliever, the fruit of unbelief. light-- of which believers are the children ( 1Th 5:5 ).
